rows.notes: The cited document is a narrative literature review (labelled 'Review' in Agricultural Water Management) with no own data, experiment, survey or validated model runs. The water-saving figures it reports (e.g. Table 1: 30%, 50%, 58.8% savings) are results of other studies (Liao et al. 2021, Wheeler et al. 2020, Guery et al. 2018) and do not count as the study's own evidence.
Review article; no primary data. Yield effects mentioned (e.g. Montesano et al. 2016 lettuce weight) are cited results of other studies, not the review's own.

Review article; no primary data. The review is about smart monitoring and control strategies, not drip irrigation per se; drip appears only incidentally in cited studies (e.g. Millan et al. 2019 plum drip).

Review article; no primary data. The hybrid model predictive control idea is presented in Section 5 and Conclusions as a research gap and future work, not as a tested result; the review itself states the impact of MPC on water use efficiency is not yet known.
Review article; no primary data. It does not discuss smartphone apps or user control panels; it summarises monitoring (soil, weather, plant) and control strategies from other studies.
Review article; no primary data. Soil health is not addressed anywhere in the review.
Review article; no primary data. Productivity/climate-change mitigation claims are not the review's own findings.
Review article; no primary data. Drought resilience is not evaluated in the review.
Review article; no primary data. Section 3.1 describes soil moisture sensors and cites other studies' outcomes; no own yield data.
Review article; no primary data. Water savings from soil moisture sensing in Table 1 are results of other studies (Liao 2021, Wheeler 2020, Guery 2018, Sui 2017).
Review article; no primary data. The review conceptually describes integration of soil, weather and plant monitoring with control strategies but reports no own measurement of water use.
Review article; no primary data on crop productivity.

Review article; the passage itself characterises it as a review. It argues (Abstract, Section 4) that closed-loop strategies are more efficient than open-loop, but this is a synthesis of cited work, not an own result.
Review article; no primary data. The statement that open-loop systems are characterised by over- and under-irrigation (Section 5) is an assertion drawn from literature, not measured.
Review article; no primary data. The passage accurately describes it as presenting closed-loop control as a route to efficiency, but there is no own evidence.

Review article; no primary data. The review does not make a specific finding about 'precautionary over-application driven by limited visibility'; it generally notes heuristic scheduling causes losses, citing Garcia et al. 2020.
Review article; no primary data. The review does not discuss reallocation of saved water or expansion of irrigated area (rebound effect); that framing is not present in the document.
Review article; no primary data. It notes drawbacks of PID, ANN and fuzzy controllers (data requirements, designer expertise) as general literature-based observations, not own findings.
Review article; no primary data. Risk management is not evaluated.

notes: The cited document is explicitly a literature review (journal section header 'Review'; title 'A review'; Conclusions describe it as a review of monitoring and control strategies). It contains no original experiment, survey, dataset or validated model run; all quantitative results (Tables 1 and 2) are attributed to other studies. Q1 is therefore 'no' for every claim row and all subsequent questions are 'no'. Full text appears complete.
